prompt:
What's the extinction cross-section of a 30 nm radius gold sphere in air at 2.5 µm wavelength? Use measured/fitted gold optical constants rather than a toy Drude model.

---
Report your result by calling submit_answer with these values:
- `c_ext_nm2` (nm^2): extinction cross-section at 2.5 um

concerns: The default gold dataset (Johnson-Christy) stops at 1937 nm, so it can't be used at 2500 nm without extrapolating. I used the Rakić et al. (1998) Lorentz-Drude fit to measured gold data instead. It covers 248–6199 nm and gives ε = −248.5 + 39.3i at 2.5 µm.

The answer depends strongly on which gold dataset you use. At this wavelength, extinction is almost entirely absorption, and absorption is roughly proportional to Im(ε). With the measured single-crystal data of Olmon et al. (2012), ε = −262.6 + 26.6i, the same Mie calculation gives C_ext = 4.56 nm² instead of 6.83 nm². Expect about ±25% uncertainty from the choice of optical constants.

These are bulk optical constants. In a 30 nm-radius particle, electrons scattering off the surface add extra damping. This raises Im(ε) and would make the absorption, and so C_ext, larger than these bulk-based values.
Other assumptions: a perfect sphere, a single particle in vacuum or air (n = 1.0) and plane-wave illumination. A sphere's response doesn't depend on polarisation. The solver gave no warnings.
answer.summary:
The extinction cross-section is about 6.83 nm² (Q_ext ≈ 0.0024). I got this from an exact Mie calculation for a 30 nm-radius gold sphere in air at 2500 nm, using the Rakić et al. Lorentz-Drude fit to measured gold data. Almost all of it is absorption (6.58 nm²); scattering is only 0.25 nm².

The value depends a lot on the gold dataset. With Olmon et al.'s measured single-crystal data, the same calculation gives 4.56 nm², because that data has a lower Im(ε) at 2.5 µm. The scattering part is the same in both cases (0.25 nm²). So a fair answer is 5–7 nm², with 6.8 nm² as the main value from the Rakić fit. Because these are bulk optical constants, they likely somewhat underestimate absorption in a particle this small.

- Lengths in nm. Wavelengths are vacuum wavelengths in nm.
- Time dependence exp(-i omega t): absorbing materials have Im(eps) > 0 and Im(n) > 0.
- Cross sections in nm^2; efficiencies Q = C / (pi r_eq^2), r_eq = volume-equivalent radius of all particles.
- layer_stack / periodic: layers listed from the superstrate (incidence side) to the substrate; light travels +z.
  R is measured in the superstrate, T in the substrate.
- mode: cross-section in the xy plane, propagation along +z.
- device: ports are planes whose normal is the axis where size_nm is zero; direction is into the device.

- Materials: {"kind": "constant_index", "n_real": .., "n_imag": ..}, {"kind": "library", "name": "Au"},
  drude, drude_lorentz, tabulated, constant_permittivity. FDTD needs dispersive models (fit_drude_lorentz).
- Results carry provenance and warnings: read the warnings before trusting the numbers.
